title: Automated Infant Wellness Reporting Using Saturation of Oxygen (SpO2) Histogram and Frequency of Desaturation in Neonates: A Feasibility Study
content: Background: Continuous physiologic monitoring produces large volumes of high-resolution data in neonatal intensive care units (NICUs), but clinicians do not rou-tinely convert these data into automated longitudinal assessments of infant physiologic wellness. Objective: To evaluate the technical and implementation feasibility of an in-tegrated digital platform (iNICU) incorporating the digital Review of Oxygen Saturation and Events (dROSE) algorithm for automated daily infant wellness reporting. Methods: We conducted a prospective, three-phase feasibility study in a quaternary NICU using seven instrumented beds. We collected heart rate, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation data at 1 Hz. dROSE applied predefined oxygen saturation and desaturation-frequency thresholds to classify daily physiologic wellness as stable, watcher, or unstable. We evaluated pre-specified feasibility criteria, compared dROSE classifications with inde-pendent bedside nurse assessments, descriptively examined subsequent clinical dete-rioration and improvement events, and assessed requirements for broader deployment using Technology Readiness Level (TRL) criteria. Results: Fifty-nine infants and 25 nurses participated. Physiologic data capture completeness was 86%, below the pre-specified 90% threshold. Following technical refinement, concordance with the reference monitoring system reached 92% for desaturation events, 91% for bradycardia events, and 90% for oxygen saturation histograms. The system auto-generated 451 eligible daily infant wellness reports. Among 126 paired assessments from 18 infants, exact agreement be-tween dROSE and bedside nurse classifications was 49.2%, with dROSE assigning a higher-severity category in 45.2%. Subsequent deterioration-event rates across nurse-assigned stable, watcher, and unstable states were 3.2, 13.2, and 15.0 events per 10 observation-days, compared with 1.4, 4.0, and 3.1 following the corresponding dROSE classifications. The team created a roadmap for broader deployment but did not carry out testing at full-unit scale. The team achieved TRL 6 with the integrated system and con-sidered it to be progressing toward TRL 7. Conclusions: The iNICU-dROSE system demonstrated pilot-scale feasibility for automated physiologic data acquisition, pro-cessing, and reporting, but limitations in acquisition reliability, high-volume reporting, and clinical concordance remain. The TRL-based assessment supports a “CONDITIONAL GO” for continued technical development, outcome-based refinement and validation of the wellness-classification approach, and targeted retesting before broader operational or clinical implementation
